explain.say: Before a new road or housing estate is built, surveyors walk a loop around the site, measuring each angle and each side, like drawing a shape with a protractor and tape. This loop is a traverse. A closed traverse ends where it began, so it carries its own check. On the board, a four-sided traverse, A, B, C, D.

explain.say: Add all the steps. A perfect loop sums to zero, but real ones never quite do. Here the east steps add to plus six centimetres and the north steps to minus eight. The gap, the closing error, is ten centimetres. Over a perimeter of five hundred and eighty two metres that is about one in five thousand eight hundred. Good enough for a building site?

explain.say: Yes, for most sites! Now share out the error with the Bowditch rule: each side is corrected in proportion to its length. Side A to B gets about minus one point six centimetres east and plus two point one north. Then the loop closes perfectly. Excellent! Challenge: with a closing error of five centimetres instead, what would the precision be?

faq.q: What is a traverse in surveying?
faq.a: A series of connected survey lines whose lengths and angles are measured. A closed traverse returns to its start or ends on a known point, so its errors can be checked and adjusted.

faq.q: What is the interior angle check for a closed traverse?
faq.a: The interior angles of a closed traverse with n sides must add to (n − 2) × 180 degrees. Any difference is the angular misclosure, shared equally among the angles if small.
asks: Sum of interior angles of a traverse

faq.a: The north-south and east-west components of each traverse leg: latitude is length times cos bearing, departure is length times sin bearing.

faq.q: How do you calculate the closing error of a traverse?
faq.a: Add all departures and all latitudes. The closing error is the square root of the sum of their squares, and dividing the perimeter by it gives the relative precision, such as 1 in 5,800.
Also called the compass rule: the misclosure in eastings and northings is distributed to each leg in proportion to its length divided by the total perimeter.

facts: The Bowditch, or compass, rule is named after the American navigator and mathematician Nathaniel Bowditch.
The interior angles of a closed traverse with n sides add up to (n − 2) × 180°.
